channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Food & Agriculture
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] FBI seizes the Chinese state-sponsored platforms that scanned critical infrastructure and relayed attacks through hijacked devices
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms run by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and tied to a Nanjing contractor. QScan performed reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed the resulting intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so traffic arrived from ordinary domestic addresses. Both platforms are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware. Named victims are federal, and the activity runs back to at least 2018. For food and agriculture the relay design is the transferable point: processing plants, cold stores and farms are full of cheap connected devices nobody patches, and that is the population these platforms recruited. - US Department of Justice press release and unsealed court documents — corroborated by TechCrunch and UPI - Seizures announced and confirmed 26 Aug 2026; described activity dates from at least 2018 to 2026

item.title: [Critical] Food and beverage ransomware volume is climbing, and production stoppages are the recurring outcome
item.category: Incident — Sector ransomware trend with production stoppages
item.description: Sector analysis published in early August tracks a continued rise in ransomware against food and beverage companies, with production stoppage rather than data theft as the characteristic consequence. The reference point remains the Fairlife incident of 16 July 2026, in which the Coca-Cola-owned dairy business suspended US production after an attack compromised systems supporting manufacturing. The pattern is consistent across the sector: attackers reach the business systems that schedule, batch, label and ship, and the line stops because it cannot run without them — not because anyone manipulated a controller. Perishability then converts an IT outage into product loss within hours rather than days. - BeverageDaily sector analysis, with the Fairlife production stoppage reported by Food Processing and Dairy Herd - Sector analysis published 3 Aug 2026; Fairlife incident 16 Jul 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] A CEVA Logistics breach reached European warehouses and rippled out through the companies it serves
item.category: Incident — Logistics breach with downstream exposure
item.description: CEVA Logistics disclosed a breach affecting European warehouse operations, with customer data spilling out through the retailers and brands it serves; reporting places the intrusion between late July and early August. Third-party logistics is where a food business’s despatch data lives — what is moving, to whom, at what temperature and on what schedule. For a processor or grower the exposure is indirect but practical: an attacker holding that data has an effective basis for social engineering against your despatch desk, your carriers and your customers, and warehouse disruption at a 3PL is a cold-chain problem long before it is a data-protection one. - TechCrunch reporting, corroborated by The Record and The Register - Attack 29 Jul – 1 Aug 2026; disclosed and reported 10–11 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Treasury sanctions an Iranian intelligence-directed hacking network operating inside US critical infrastructure
item.category: Incident — Nation-state targeting of US critical infrastructure
item.description: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security-directed hacking network on 24 August as part of a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels, with a related State Department reward notice. Treasury states the network has breached and exfiltrated data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. Food and agriculture is not named. What transfers is tradecraft rather than targeting: harvesting credentials, exploiting supplier footholds and collecting network documentation works the same way against a processing plant, and food businesses typically carry a long list of integrators and equipment suppliers with standing access. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; Department of Justice indictment; State Department Rewards for Justice notice — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop and Nextgov/FCW - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; press analysis 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Refrigeration controllers can be switched off while the temperature display keeps reading normal
item.category: Threat intel — Refrigeration controller research with vendor advisories
item.description: Claroty’s Team82 published research into commercial refrigeration controllers, with corresponding advisories from Danfoss and Copeland. The finding that matters to a food business is not remote access in itself but the divergence between what the controller does and what the operator sees: cooling can be disabled or setpoints altered while the display continues to report a normal temperature. That is a food-safety failure mode dressed as a security finding. Every HACCP monitoring assumption you hold rests on the reading being true, and a compromised controller breaks the assumption silently — there is no alarm, because the system reporting the alarm is the system that was changed. - Claroty Team82 research; Danfoss and Copeland vendor advisories — reported by SecurityWeek - Research and advisories reported 14 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Dragos counts 70 food and beverage ransomware incidents in a single quarter
item.category: Threat intel — Quarterly industrial ransomware analysis
item.description: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in Q2 2026, up around 12 percent on Q1, with 70 of them in food and beverage. The analysis is direct about mechanism: attackers did not need control-system access to disrupt production. Encrypting ERP, MES, labelling, warehouse management and scheduling stops a line as effectively as touching a PLC and takes far less skill. For food businesses the compounding factor is time. A manufacturer of durable goods loses schedule; a food processor loses product, and the recovery clock is set by shelf life and by the regulatory records that have to accompany whatever was in progress. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Dragos and Help Net Security - Report covers Q2 2026; published and reported 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
item.category: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings
item.description: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes paired red-team results from two critical-infrastructure organisations assessed with comparable tradecraft. One detected and responded; the other never noticed a domain compromise. The advisory is unusually direct that the difference was not product spend — both had capable tooling, but only one reviewed the output, correlated identity events and had practised the response. Food manufacturers will recognise the shape: plant systems and corporate IT commonly share one Active Directory, monitoring is frequently outsourced to a small provider, and the production estate is often excluded from detection because the alerts were judged too noisy. - CISA cybersecurity advisory AA26-237A — joint red-team assessment findings, corroborated by CyberScoop - Published 25 Aug 2026; verified against the CISA advisory 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from a patching recommendation to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, requiring no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept. In food manufacturing NetScaler commonly fronts the remote access used by plant engineers, out-of-hours support and the OEMs who dial in to fillers, packaging lines and refrigeration. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 and Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — corroborated by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and watchTowr Labs analysis - Vendor bulletin published 20 Aug 2026; exploitation indications from 17 Aug; added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] A Git server exploit in KEV — and it is often where recipe and line configuration lives
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, engineering toolchain
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August after reports of active exploitation. Rated CVSS 9.8, the flaw lets anyone with ordinary repository write access plant an executable Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Gitea 1.27.1 fixed it on 27 July, so exploitation followed within a month. Self-hosted Gitea appears in food plants more often than people expect, stood up by controls engineering to hold PLC projects, HMI screens, recipe parameter sets and integration scripts. A low-privilege contractor account then becomes code execution on the machine holding your line configuration. Federal remediation was due 28 August. - CISA KEV catalogue addition — corroborated by Help Net Security, SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Gitea 1.27.1 released 27 Jul 2026; added to KEV 25 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CVSS 10.0 on a Siemens edge gateway that is dual-homed by design
item.category: Advisory — Maximum severity, Siemens edge gateway
item.description: Siemens’ August advisory set includes a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices, allowing a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute code with elevated privileges. Ten Siemens advisories arrived in the same batch alongside Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact publications. The relevance in a food plant is placement rather than score. Edge gateways are installed specifically to move line data out to an OEE platform, a corporate historian or a supplier cloud service, which makes them dual-homed by design and frequently the one device with a route between the production network and everything else. - Siemens ProductCERT August 2026 advisories and the CISA ICS advisory batch — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Fire-alarm management software stores its credentials in cleartext in memory, CISA warns
item.category: Advisory — Cleartext credentials in fire-alarm management software
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-232-01, republishing Johnson Controls advisory JCI-PSA-2026-28, covers a flaw in Simplex Incident Manager fire-alarm management software that stores credentials in cleartext in memory, where a local attacker or malicious process could recover them. It is not a remote code execution finding, but it sits in a life-safety system, and in a food plant fire-alarm management usually shares a network and often a server estate with access control, refrigeration monitoring and building services. Recovered credentials from one of those systems are typically valid across several of them. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01; Johnson Controls product security advisory JCI-PSA-2026-28 - Published 20 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] No login required and no patch coming — the Ebyte gateway advisory is a replacement decision
item.category: Advisory — Serial-to-Ethernet gateway, no vendor patch
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-237-06 covers the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, whose web management interface does not consistently enforce authentication before granting administrative functionality. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read configuration, change settings, hijack sessions or disrupt operation. CISA notes the vendor acknowledged the reports, said a patch was in development, then stopped responding. Cheap serial converters of this class are everywhere in food and agriculture: behind older scales and checkweighers, batch controllers, grain moisture meters, bin monitors, milk tank sensors and cold-store loggers — installed because something legacy needed a network drop. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-237-06, reported by researcher Jithin Nambiar — via CISA - Published 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026 — no vendor patch announced

item.title: [High] An exploited Windows IKE flaw — pre-authentication SYSTEM on the box terminating your site-to-site VPN
item.category: Advisory — Exploited Windows IKE flaw in KEV
item.description: CISA added four exploited vulnerabilities to KEV on 18 August, including a Windows Internet Key Exchange flaw permitting pre-authentication code execution as SYSTEM. Microsoft shipped the fix in April, so the gap is deployment rather than availability. Placement is what makes it relevant to a food business: IKE runs on the hosts terminating site-to-site tunnels, and those tunnels are how head office reaches a plant, how a plant reaches a distribution centre or a farm operation, and how an OEM reaches packaging equipment through a concentrator. Compromise there puts an attacker at the junction of both networks. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue and Microsoft security updates — via CISA and The Hacker News - Added to CISA KEV 18 Aug 2026; vendor patch issued April 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] From 11 September 2026 exploited vulnerabilities in digital products must be reported within 24 hours
item.category: Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligation
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations begin on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability in their product, or a severe incident affecting its security, within 24 hours of becoming aware, with fuller reporting to follow. Food and agriculture businesses are mostly buyers here, and that is the useful angle: the suppliers of fillers, packaging lines, refrigeration controllers, weighing systems and ag-IoT platforms sold into Europe acquire a defined notification duty that can be written into support contracts. - European Commission guidance on Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations (Regulation 2024/2847) - Regulation entered into force 10 Dec 2024; reporting obligations apply from 11 Sep 2026; full application 11 Dec 2027; status verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] The NSA is putting an ISA/IEC 62443 certificate in front of the controllers it buys
item.description: ISASecure announced a partnership with the National Security Agency to develop a High Criticality Component Security Assurance certification scheme, derived from its Component Security Assurance programme and grounded in ISA/IEC 62443-4-2. Once accepted, the NSA intends to use it when adding OT components to the National Security Systems product compliant list. Food producers are not the target market, but the mechanism matters: a large buyer making certification a purchase condition changes what vendors build, and the language migrates into other specifications. For a business writing a filler, packaging or refrigeration tender, that is a citable standard rather than an invented requirement. - ISA / ISASecure press release — corroborated by Automation World and ISSSource - Announced 20 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026
